I did a few hackathons at the intersection of AI and web3, built small things, broke them, and spent a lot of time thinking about what comes next. I also started a boardgame content page on Instagram with friends, @theboardgameboulevard, and finished Hyrox doubles, which is my biggest flex right now. Before that I spent five years building ecosystems in India. I started The Phoenix Guild in 2022, a diversity-first builder community that eventually ran across 13 chapters and got a lot of people their first crypto job. It's not running anymore but it's still the thing I'm proudest of. Then Hashed Emergent, where I worked on accelerator programs and India Blockchain Week, and then Aptos, where I built out the India ecosystem and later moved into a global role supporting founders. Most of that work was the unglamorous side of growth. Getting builders in the door, keeping them there, and figuring out which programs actually moved a number versus which ones just looked good in a recap post. That's what I'm good at, so I started digging into how AI companies acquire and keep their users, and I'm going to write it up. One company a week, how they grow, where it leaks, and what I'd change. Most of them will be AI companies because that's where I'm spending my time now. I haven't left crypto though, so if you're building there I'd still love to hear from you. First one is Instinct, the assistant you text. They're reportedly raising at a valuation of $10 billion, and the founder shares percentages and averages about users but never how many there are. firms-implementing-ai-apprenticeship-rep.text: Firms Implementing AI Apprenticeship Replacement - Training Playbook | Journo Request Sourcee Open main menu Features Pricing Reviews FAQ Log in Start free trial Posted in last 7 days Firms Implementing AI Apprenticeship Replacement - Training Playbook I have spent three weeks complaining, so here is the constructive half. How do we fix the looming training crisis that AI is causing? The test is not “keep the boring work and hope for the best”. Nobody should defend obsolete tasks for their own sake. The test is: Does this replace what the old task was secretly teaching? Can it help build the experience that makes humans so adaptable? I think there are four things, all of which already exist somewhere, none of which any firm I can find has assembled in one place One. Borrow the architecture school’s crit. (thanks Alfonso Padro for that one!) Make trainees defend the machine’s answer, aloud, to someone senior. Do not assess the document. Assess whether they understand why it is right. Two. Plant known errors in the machine’s output and reward juniors for finding them. Flight simulators have thrown engineered emergencies at pilots for decades. We need manufactured mistakes in places where being wrong is free. (Star Trek fans should think Jim Kirk and the Kobayashi Maru simulation...) Three. Replay real work. Take a closed case, transaction, audit or investigation. Remove the advice and the outcome, then give the trainee the evidence in the order it originally appeared. At each stage, make them commit: What matters? What is missing? What would you do next? Then show them what actually happened. That gives young lawyers and accountants something AI threatens to deny them: a bank of remembered situations against which to test the unfamiliar. Four. Put the trainee in charge of the machine. Give them a complete but bounded piece of work. They decide what to delegate to AI, what must be checked, what requires human investigation and when to escalate. A senior remains accountable, but assesses the trainee’s decisions, not merely the document that emerges at the end. The objective is not to teach juniors how to use AI. It is to teach them how to be responsible for work produced with AI. Hand over the responsibility to them in stages. None of this is exotic. What does not yet exist, as far as I can find, is the firm that has put the pieces together deliberately, as the replacement for the apprenticeship it has just automated away.
